# Optical fibre communication (`optical_fibre`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/electricity.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Electricity & electronics (`electricity`)
- Deps: needs clear_glass, refraction_optics; helped by laser, information_theory
- Core idea: Light inside glass that meets the surface at a shallow angle is totally reflected, so a thin glass thread guides light round bends. It works over distance only if the thread has a core of slightly higher refractive index inside a cladding of lower index, so that the light never touches the outer surface. Ordinary glass loses the light within metres, but the loss is caused by impurities, mainly iron and other metals and traces of water, not by glass itself. Fused silica made from purified vapour, with the impurities at parts per thousand million, carries infrared light for many kilometres. A core only a few thousandths of a millimetre wide and a semiconductor laser switched on and off very rapidly then carry far more telephone calls than any copper cable or microwave link.
- Pitfalls:
  - A bare glass thread without cladding: light leaks wherever it is touched or dirty
  - Assuming glass is too absorbing in principle; that was the general opinion until Kao showed in 1966 that the loss comes from removable impurities
  - Purifying by melting in crucibles, which adds impurities; the working method deposits silica from vapour
  - Looking into the end of a live fibre; the infrared beam is invisible and can damage the eye
- History: europe: 1841–1842 – Colladon (Geneva) and Babinet guide light in a water jet, popularised by Tyndall in 1854; 1954 van Heel (Delft) and Hopkins and Kapany (London) publish on clad fibres and image bundles; 1966 Kao and Hockham (Standard Telecommunication Laboratories, Harlow) show that low-loss fibre is possible; americas: 1970 – Maurer, Keck and Schultz at Corning make fibre with a loss below 20 decibels per kilometre; 1977 first telephone traffic over fibre (Chicago, Long Beach); 1988 TAT-8 transatlantic fibre cable
- Read:
  - K. C. Kao & G. A. Hockham, Dielectric-fibre surface waveguides for optical frequencies, Proceedings of the IEE 113 (1966)
  - Jeff Hecht, City of Light: The Story of Fiber Optics (1999)
